title: Conflict between Mavis and Delroy
source:
(A small living room. Evening. A folded heap of clothes on the table.)

MAVIS: (folding) You are not going to that party, Delroy.
DELROY: Mama, I am seventeen. Everybody in my class is going.
MAVIS: Everybody is not my child. Your father would turn in his grave if he knew I let you stay out until morning.
DELROY: (quietly) Do not talk about Papa as if you own his memory.
MAVIS: (stops folding; a long silence) What did you say to me?
DELROY: I said I am going. (He picks up a parcel from the table.)
MAVIS: Put that down.
DELROY: It is mine. I bought it with my own money, from what Uncle Cecil pays me at the shop.
MAVIS: (sitting) So that is how it is now. You have your own money, so you have your own house.
DELROY: (at the door, not looking back) Mama. It is one night.
MAVIS: Then go. And when you come back you will find the door locked, and you will know what it cost.
(He leaves. She sits for a long moment, then goes to the door and unbolts it.)
prompt: Write an essay in which you discuss how the playwright presents the conflict between Mavis and Delroy, and explain the effect of that conflict on the audience.
planningHints: Decide what the conflict is really about - permission, grief, money, or a mother's fear - and say so in your introduction.
Choose three or four moments (the opening refusal, the reference to Papa, the money, the threat and the unbolting) and build a paragraph on each.
Always name the technique and then explain the effect: dialogue, stage directions, silence, the final stage picture.
modelAnswer:
The extract stages a conflict that begins as an argument about a party and turns out to be about authority, grief and a boy's growing independence. The playwright builds it almost entirely out of dialogue and silence, so the audience watches two people hurt each other without either of them being made the villain.

The conflict opens with two flat statements - 'You are not going' against 'Mama, I am seventeen' - and the brevity of the lines makes the two wills sound equally fixed. Mavis's appeal to the dead father, 'your father would turn in his grave', introduces the real subject, and Delroy's reply, 'Do not talk about Papa as if you own his memory', is the turning point of the scene.

The playwright marks that turning point with a stage direction rather than a speech: '(stops folding; a long silence)'. The silence tells the audience that Mavis is wounded rather than merely disobeyed, and it shifts our sympathy, so that we feel the grief behind her control. Her next words, 'So that is how it is now. You have your own money, so you have your own house', give the conflict an economic edge: an ordinary parcel becomes a symbol of independence, and a wage becomes a threat to her place in his life.

The climax is the mother's threat to lock the door, which is both punishment and an admission of fear. The playwright then resolves the scene without a word: '(She sits for a long moment, then goes to the door and unbolts it.)' That final stage picture is devastating because the audience understands what Mavis will never say - her love outlasts her anger - and we are left with the tension unresolved, since Delroy does not know that the door is open.
markScheme: Content and understanding (10 marks): accurate knowledge of the extract; a clear line of argument about the nature of the conflict and its effect.
Analysis of technique (10 marks): discussion of dialogue, stage directions, silence and stage pictures, with explanation of the effects created.
Use of evidence (5 marks): brief, well-chosen quotations and stage directions embedded in the argument.
Organisation and expression (5 marks): purposeful paragraphs, connectives between points, accurate written English and consistent tense.
examinerTips: In the examination you will write on your set play, but the skills are the same: talk about how the scene is staged, not only what the characters say. A paragraph with no stage direction in it is usually a paragraph about plot.

title: Character revealed in the staff room
source:
(A primary school staff room. The lamp is broken; afternoon light comes through the louvres. A box of unmarked papers stands on the desk.)

PRINCIPAL: Two Grade 6 students wrote no mathematics test last week. Their parents say the class had no teacher.
MISS ANN: That is true, sir. Miss Clarke left in May and nobody was sent in her place.
PRINCIPAL: (reading a letter) Then we do what we can with who we have. (pause) I have recommended you for both classes.
MISS ANN: Both? Sir, I already teach Grade 4 and Grade 5, and I mark the whole school's papers.
PRINCIPAL: I know what you already do. (He looks up for the first time.)
MISS ANN: (after a moment) Then I will need the past papers by Friday. And someone to mark Grade 5 on Tuesdays.
PRINCIPAL: (writing) I will ask Mr Thomas. He owes me a favour.
MISS ANN: He owes you three years of favours. (She takes the letter from his desk and reads it.)
PRINCIPAL: (quietly) The Ministry has not said yes. It is only a request. Do not build on it.
MISS ANN: Then I will not build on it. I will do the term. After that I make no promise either.
(She folds the letter and puts it in her bag. A bell rings off stage.)
prompt: Write an essay in which you discuss how the playwright uses dialogue and stage directions to reveal the characters of Miss Ann and the Principal.
planningHints: Work character by character or technique by technique - dialogue, stage directions, silence, the handling of objects - but keep answering the question.
Notice what the characters refuse to say as well as what they say.
Use the objects in the scene (the letter, the unmarked papers, the broken lamp) as evidence.
modelAnswer:
The playwright builds these two characters out of the way they speak to each other, and out of a handful of stage directions. Neither is caricatured: the scene leaves the audience respecting Miss Ann and understanding the Principal's bind.

The Principal is first revealed by indirection. He reports the problem passively - 'their parents say the class had no teacher' - and the direction '(reading a letter)' shows a man attending to paper rather than people. When he finally looks up, the playwright marks it as an event: '(He looks up for the first time.)' Presenting his request as something he has already 'recommended' shows a manager who prefers decisions to be finished before they are discussed. His admission, 'I know what you already do', is honest and, coming after the pause, suggests discomfort rather than indifference.

Miss Ann is revealed through precise, practical speech. She answers with facts - 'Miss Clarke left in May' - and does not complain about her workload; she prices it: 'the past papers by Friday', 'someone to mark Grade 5'. Her wit, 'He owes you three years of favours', shows intelligence and courage, and the stage direction that she takes the letter from his desk is the moment the audience sees that she, not he, is the one who will act on it. Reading it herself also shows that she has stopped accepting authority on trust.

The playwright reserves the strongest characterisation for what is withheld. The Principal lowers his voice - '(quietly) The Ministry has not said yes' - because he has offered a colleague more work on no authority. Miss Ann's reply, 'I will do the term. After that I make no promise either', is not defiance but self-protection, and the audience recognises a professional who has learned to protect herself from the institution she serves. When the bell rings off stage and the scene ends without either of them moving, the playwright leaves us with two tired people holding a school together.
markScheme: Content and understanding (10 marks): accurate knowledge of the extract and a clear line of argument about both characters.
Analysis of technique (10 marks): use of dialogue, stage directions, pauses and props to reveal character, with effects explained.
Use of evidence (5 marks): short embedded quotations and stage directions.
Organisation and expression (5 marks): balanced treatment of both characters, purposeful paragraphs, accurate English.
examinerTips: Character questions ask how the character is presented, not what happens to them. Notice the playwright's objects as well as the speeches: who holds the letter matters as much as what is in it.

title: The coming of rain
source:
NIGHT RAIN, ST ELIZABETH

The hills put on their darkest cloth
and wait. Then the rain comes down
like a long argument settled at last,
filling the dry gut with silver,
drumming the galvanise into applause.

By morning the yam vines are jewelled,
the road is a river with opinions,
and old Mr Bailey, who has prayed
for forty years without an answer,
stands in his doorway and says nothing at all.
prompt: Write an essay in which you discuss how the poet's use of figurative language presents the coming of the rain and its effect on the people of the district.
planningHints: Track the poem in order: waiting, arriving, morning, the human response.
Name each device, quote it briefly, state the picture it creates, then link it to the theme.
Ask what the last two lines do that no earlier line does.
modelAnswer:
The poem presents the arrival of rain as both a physical event and an answer to long waiting, and it does so through a chain of images that grow from the natural world into human feeling.

The opening line uses personification: the hills 'put on their darkest cloth and wait'. Dressing the hills as a person preparing for something gives the landscape a deliberate stillness, and the verb 'wait' makes the reader wait too. The simile that follows, the rain coming down 'like a long argument settled at last', is striking because it compares a storm to a resolution: what pounds the roof is also relief, and the phrase 'settled at last' suggests a quarrel that has lasted years. The metaphor 'filling the dry gut with silver' turns muddy water into treasure, and 'drumming the galvanise into applause' makes the sound of rain an audience clapping - the district itself is celebrating.

The second stanza shifts from the storm to its aftermath. 'The yam vines are jewelled' continues the imagery of wealth, and 'the road is a river with opinions' is a playful metaphor that gives the flooded road a voice; the land is now active and talkative, where before it was silent and waiting. That personification prepares the reader for the poem's real interest, which is not the weather but the people.

The final image is the heart of the poem. Mr Bailey 'who has prayed for forty years without an answer' stands in his doorway 'and says nothing at all'. The words 'without an answer' and the loudness of the storm are placed against his silence, so that the rain appears to him as the answer he has stopped expecting. Because the poet does not tell us how he feels, the reader supplies the feeling, and the poem becomes a quiet statement about endurance, faith and the difference between weather and grace.
markScheme: Content and understanding (10 marks): clear account of the poem's movement from storm to morning to Mr Bailey.
Analysis of figurative language (10 marks): personification, simile and metaphor identified, quoted and their effects explained.
Use of evidence and structure (5 marks): brief quotations; comment on the two-stanza structure and the closing image.
Organisation and expression (5 marks): purposeful paragraphs and accurate critical vocabulary.
examinerTips: Naming a device is worth one mark at most; the effect is worth the rest. Always finish an analysis sentence with what the image makes the reader think or feel.

title: Tone and loss in 'For the One Who Left'
source:
FOR THE ONE WHO LEFT

You took the good scissors and the blue bowl,
the calendar with everybody's birthdays on it.
You left the key under the flowerpot
because that is where we always left it,
and you left the door unlocked.

I have not moved the flowerpot.
I water it in the dry season, the way you taught me,
and the key stays under it, warm as a coin,
in case you come back the way you left -
walking, in the morning, saying nothing.
prompt: Write an essay in which you discuss how the poet presents the theme of loss and how the poem's tone and structure shape the reader's response.
planningHints: Distinguish the theme (loss) from the tone (how the speaker feels about it), and be prepared to say that the tone is not simply sad.
Notice the ordinary objects and the repetition of 'left'; ask what is missing from the poem.
Consider the shape: five lines, five lines; moving from what was taken to what is kept.
modelAnswer:
The poem is about loss, but its most striking quality is how little it accuses anyone. The speaker grieves quietly, and the poem's power comes from restraint: the absence is presented honestly and forgiven before the reader can condemn.

The first stanza catalogues what the departed person did. The objects are deliberately ordinary - 'the good scissors', 'the blue bowl', 'the calendar with everybody's birthdays on it' - and it is the calendar that hurts, since it was the household's record of belonging. The verb 'left' is repeated three times, which makes departure the subject of the poem, and there is a fine distinction between taking and leaving: what was taken was property, but what was left - the key, the unlocked door - is an invitation.

The second stanza turns to the speaker's own behaviour, and its tone is tender rather than bitter. The line 'I have not moved the flowerpot' is an act of devotion disguised as an admission of stubbornness, and 'I water it in the dry season, the way you taught me' is both an act of love and an insistence that the departed one is still present in everyday habits. The simile 'warm as a coin' gives the hidden key a living quality, and 'the key stays under it' suggests that the speaker is holding time still.

The poem ends with the only wish it contains - 'in case you come back the way you left' - completed by the most restrained line in the poem, 'walking, in the morning, saying nothing'. The dashes delay that line, and its subject is not apology or explanation but a return so ordinary it needs no words. This is where the theme and the tone meet: the loss is not denied, and the forgiveness is complete before it is asked for. Ten short lines, five to grieve and five to hope, and the reader is left wanting to know whether the door was ever used again.
markScheme: Content and understanding (10 marks): a clear reading of the poem's two-part movement and its treatment of departure and waiting.
Analysis of tone and technique (10 marks): discussion of diction, repetition, ordinary objects and restraint, with effects explained.
Use of evidence and structure (5 marks): short quotations; comment on stanza shape, the simile and the final delayed line.
Organisation and expression (5 marks): argument sustained across paragraphs; accurate critical language.
examinerTips: Tone questions are often answered with one word - sad, hopeful - which earns almost nothing. Show how the diction creates the tone and how the tone changes across the poem.

title: Comparing two poems on home and distance
source:
ISLAND, 6 A.M.

Here the sea is a rooster
and the bread van is the alarm.
Everybody's grandmother knows your name.
You will never be famous here,
which is either a wound or a mercy,
depending on the morning.

- - -

NORTH, 6 A.M.

Here the sea is a car park
and the bread van does not come.
Nobody's grandmother knows your name.
You can be anybody here,
which is either a mercy or a wound,
depending on the morning.
prompt: Write an essay in which you compare the two poems, considering how each poet presents the experience of home and of living away from it.
planningHints: Choose a shared basis for comparison - the treatment of community, identity or belonging - and organise your essay around it, moving between the poems.
Notice the reversing structure: the same lines reappear with one idea swapped. Say what that reversal does.
Use connectives: 'whereas', 'similarly', 'in contrast', 'both'.
modelAnswer:
The two poems are built on an obvious symmetry: six lines each, the same daily hour, and a closing line that is almost identical - except that 'wound' and 'mercy' exchange places. This mirroring invites the reader to compare belonging at home with anonymity abroad, and it suggests that neither experience is simply better than the other.

Both poems begin with the sea, but the imagery could not be more different. In 'Island' the sea is 'a rooster', a metaphor that makes it noisy and alive and part of the domestic routine, and the morning is marked by 'the bread van', the sound of community. In 'North' the sea is 'a car park', a flat, unromantic comparison that suggests a place organised for machines, and 'the bread van does not come', so there is no daily ritual to belong to. The contrast prepares the reader for the poems' central idea: life at home is full of people, and life away is full of space.

The third line turns the comparison into a statement about identity. 'Everybody's grandmother knows your name' is warm but limiting, while 'Nobody's grandmother knows your name' is lonely but freeing, and the following line makes that paradox explicit: 'You will never be famous here' against 'You can be anybody here'. In other words, one poem describes a place where you are known and cannot escape your history, and the other a place where you are unknown and can reinvent yourself.

What lifts both poems beyond a simple complaint is the final line, in which the order of 'wound' and 'mercy' is reversed and qualified by 'depending on the morning'. The reversal works because both speakers need the same two words; they differ only in the order in which they feel them. The poems therefore read as two halves of one experience - migration is loss and opportunity at once - and the repeated closing line shows that the speaker's judgement is not fixed but daily, which is both honest and moving.
markScheme: Content and understanding (10 marks): clear comparison of the two poems' treatment of home and distance.
Analysis of technique (10 marks): discussion of metaphor, parallelism, repetition and the reversal of the closing line, with effects explained.
Comparison skills (5 marks): a shared basis for comparison; the essay moves between the poems throughout rather than describing them one after the other.
Organisation and expression (5 marks): connectives, purposeful paragraphs and accurate English.
examinerTips: Examining two poems one after the other under a heading like 'Poem 1' and 'Poem 2' cannot score comparison marks. Compare point by point, even if you quote each poem only once per paragraph.

title: Cecil arrives in the district
source:
When the bus finally reached the gap in the road, the driver did not switch off the engine. He leaned across and shouted the name of the district, twice, then sat back and waited with the patience of a man who has been shouted at by everyone.

Cecil stepped down into a darkness that was not quite dark. The air smelled of rain on hot stones and of something sweet going over. Somewhere behind the shop a dog began to bark and then thought better of it. He set down his bag - it contained everything he owned except his father's cutlass, which was too long to travel with and lay now under his mother's bed - and he looked at the two lit windows, one of them his aunt's, and he could not tell which.
prompt: Write an essay in which you discuss how the writer creates atmosphere and presents Cecil's state of mind at this moment.
planningHints: Collect the details that appeal to the senses, and say what each one contributes to the atmosphere.
Ask what the cutlass tells us about Cecil's past and his present.
The last sentence is the key: consider why the writer makes the lit windows indistinguishable.
modelAnswer:
The passage describes a homecoming without a home, and the writer creates an atmosphere of uncertainty through the senses and through one image of helplessness at the end.

The scene begins with the bus and its impatient driver, who 'did not switch off the engine' and shouts the district's name 'twice'. This is not a welcome. The engine running, the shouting and the man's weary patience give the arrival the atmosphere of a stop along a route rather than a return, and the reader is prepared for a character who is not expected by anyone.

Atmosphere is then built from impressions that are deliberately incomplete: a darkness that is 'not quite dark', air that smells of 'rain on hot stones and of something sweet going over'. Both smells belong to the Caribbean evening, but the second is also the smell of decay, so the comfort and the threat arrive together. The dog that barks 'and then thought better of it' is a small, sharp detail that makes the night feel watchful, as though the district is observing Cecil without deciding about him.

The bag is where the writer places Cecil's history. It holds everything he owns except his father's cutlass, which is 'too long to travel with' and 'lay now under his mother's bed' - so the reader learns in one sentence that the father is gone, that the mother remains, and that the son has left both behind. The cutlass is also the tool of a working man, and its absence suggests that Cecil cannot practise here what he practised at home.

The final sentence delivers the passage's meaning: looking at 'the two lit windows, one of them his aunt's', Cecil 'could not tell which'. Two identical lights, one correct and one wrong, perfectly represent a boy who belongs to a family he cannot identify from the outside. The writer never states that Cecil is frightened or hopeful, but the setting does the work, and the reader is left with a character standing at the edge of light, unsure which door is his.
markScheme: Content and understanding (10 marks): clear account of atmosphere and of what the passage reveals about Cecil.
Analysis of technique (10 marks): sensory imagery, contrast, symbolism (the cutlass, the two lit windows) and the significance of the closing sentence.
Use of evidence (5 marks): short embedded quotations from the extract.
Organisation and expression (5 marks): paragraphs that develop an argument about the writing rather than retelling the arrival.
examinerTips: Questions on atmosphere require you to discuss the senses and to explain the feeling they build. Never just list the smells and sounds.

title: The narrator who explains himself
source:
I will tell you what happened, and you can decide.

I was not on the verandah that evening. I was at the shop, which I have told the police, and they wrote it down. What I did not tell them - because nobody asked - is that the shop closes at seven and I stayed on the step until nearly eight because the rain had started. If anyone had walked up the hill between seven and eight, I would have seen them. That is all I am saying. I am not saying who it was. Somebody in this village knows that I could have said a name, and I have chosen not to, and that is a kindness and not a weakness.
prompt: Write an essay in which you discuss how the first-person narrator shapes the reader's judgement of him.
planningHints: Note what the narrator insists on: his position, the time, his silence and his motives.
Look for the gaps - what he does not tell the police and what he will not say.
Decide whether the reader trusts him, and be ready to argue why the writer makes that decision difficult.
modelAnswer:
The narrator speaks directly to the reader, explaining and defending himself, and the writer uses that first-person voice to make the reader a judge who cannot be entirely satisfied.

The opening sentence, 'I will tell you what happened, and you can decide', hands over both the account and the verdict. It sounds generous, but it also places a duty on the reader that the narrator avoids himself. He then builds an alibi from careful facts - he was at the shop, he told the police, 'and they wrote it down' - as though the record proves his innocence. The phrase 'which I have told the police' is defensible, yet the reader notices that he is quoting himself as a witness in his own case.

The most revealing sentence is the admission that he stayed on the step until nearly eight 'because the rain had started'. His position is now the best possible vantage point on the hill, and, by putting himself there, he explains how he could have 'seen them' - a phrase that reveals he does have knowledge while appearing to prove nothing. Because he tells us the second half of the truth only after he has assured us of the first, the writer makes the reader suspect a controlled confession: honesty and concealment at the same time.

His refusal to name anyone is the crux of the passage. 'I am not saying who it was' could be loyalty, fear or guilt, and the narrator supplies his own defence - 'a kindness and not a weakness' - which only invites the reader to test it. That defence also reveals his pride, since it insists that he had the power to name someone, and it flatters the village with the idea that he has protected it.

Finally, because a first-person narrator can tell us only what he chooses, the reader's suspicion grows not from any evidence against him but from the shape of his speech. The writer leaves the question open, so the passage becomes an examination of self-justification: a man who asks to be trusted tells us exactly why we hesitate.
markScheme: Content and understanding (10 marks): a clear reading of the narrator and of the passage's effect.
Analysis of point of view (10 marks): direct address, self-justification, selective disclosure, gaps and ambiguity, with effects explained.
Use of evidence (5 marks): short quotations embedded smoothly in the argument.
Organisation and expression (5 marks): a clear line of argument about the narrator, sustained and concluded.
examinerTips: For point-of-view questions, look for what the narrator chooses not to say. An unreliable narrator is usually revealed by gaps and by the way he argues, not by contradictions.

title: Persuasion in an editorial: 'Let the children play'
source:
LET THE CHILDREN PLAY

Every afternoon, thousands of children in this country are locked out of the one place built for them: the community playing field. The drain covers are missing. The lights have been dark for two years. And in those same parishes, we read of idle youth and wonder why.

We have spent millions on stadia that host three matches a year, while the field where a boy learns to keep his temper is left to goats and weeds. A football costs four thousand dollars. A stadium costs four hundred million. Which investment produces a citizen?

I have coached for eleven years. I have seen a boy arrive angry and leave a captain. I have never met a child whose life was made better by being chased off a field; I have met plenty who were made worse by being chased away from everything.

The money exists. The need is documented. What is missing is the will to spend a little of it on the small places and the small people, whose only crime is being young and having nowhere to go. Fund the fields.
prompt: Write an essay in which you analyse the persuasive techniques used in this editorial and evaluate how convincing you find it.
planningHints: Identify the claim first, then sort the techniques into appeals to reason, to the writer's authority and to emotion.
Quote the techniques briefly and explain what each one is trying to make the reader do.
For the evaluation, say which evidence is strong and which is vague, and end with a clear judgement.
modelAnswer:
The editorial argues that community playing fields, not grand stadia, deserve public money, and it persuades by combining rhetorical structure, appeals to emotion and a claim on the writer's own experience.

The opening paragraph uses a metaphor - children are 'locked out of the one place built for them' - and follows it with two short, factual statements, 'The drain covers are missing' and 'The lights have been dark for two years'. The blunt syntax makes neglect sound like recorded fact, and the paragraph ends with a rhetorical question, 'we read of idle youth and wonder why', which invites the reader to supply the answer the writer cannot be bothered to spell out.

The second paragraph makes the strongest appeal to reason through contrast and figures: millions for stadia that 'host three matches a year' against a field left 'to goats and weeds', and the deliberate arithmetic of 'A football costs four thousand dollars. A stadium costs four hundred million.' The question that follows, 'Which investment produces a citizen?', is a rhetorical question that turns a budget debate into a moral one.

Emotion and personal authority are then used together. 'I have coached for eleven years' establishes ethos, while the antithesis 'made better by being chased off a field' against 'made worse by being chased away from everything' uses repetition and wordplay to make the reader feel the unfairness. The description of the children as 'the small people, whose only crime is being young and having nowhere to go' is deeply emotive, and the final command, 'Fund the fields', gives the piece the shape of an action, not an opinion.

The editorial is persuasive, but it is not entirely convincing. The emotional appeal is powerful and the detail about drain covers and lights is specific and checkable, yet the financial claims are vague - 'millions', 'four hundred million' - with no source, and the argument rests partly on the writer's own testimony, which cannot be verified. A reader who supports youth sport will be moved; a reader who asks for costs and evidence will notice that the editorial prefers feeling to proof, which weakens the case it is trying so hard to win.
markScheme: Content and understanding (10 marks): accurate identification of the claim and the argument's structure.
Analysis of persuasive technique (10 marks): metaphor, syntax, rhetorical questions, contrast, repetition, ethos and emotive language, with effects explained.
Use of evidence (5 marks): brief, well-chosen quotations that support the analysis.
Evaluation and judgement (5 marks): a supported judgement on how convincing the piece is, distinguishing strong from weak evidence.
examinerTips: Questions that ask you to evaluate need a judgement. Present the strengths, then the weaknesses, then say where you stand and why.

title: Creative response: the scene after the door was unbolted
source:
Recall these two moments.

From the drama extract: MAVIS: Then go. And when you come back you will find the door locked, and you will know what it cost. (He leaves. She sits for a long moment, then goes to the door and unbolts it.)

From the prose extract: He looked at the two lit windows, one of them his aunt's, and he could not tell which.
prompt: Write a creative response of about 300-400 words. Choose ONE of the following. (a) Write the scene that follows, in which Delroy returns home before dawn. Use dialogue and at least three stage directions. (b) Write a paragraph in which Cecil chooses a door and knocks. Use sensory detail and keep the third-person point of view. Then add a short commentary (about 80 words) explaining three choices you made as a writer and why.
planningHints: Decide the emotion you want the reader to feel at the end, and work backwards.
Borrow the techniques of the original: silence, ordinary objects, sensory detail, a final image that carries the feeling.
In your commentary, name the techniques you used - it is part of the marks.
modelAnswer:
(Model response to option (a).)

(The living room, hours later. The folded clothes are still on the table. The lamp is switched off. MAVIS is asleep in the chair, her hand on the armrest.)

MAVIS: (waking suddenly, without moving) The door is open.
DELROY: (from the doorway) Mama.
MAVIS: I did not hear the bus.
DELROY: I walked. From the junction.
(A pause. He is still holding the parcel.)
MAVIS: You walked. Two miles, in the dark, to tell me something.
DELROY: To put this on the table.
(He unwraps the parcel. It is a small radio, still in its box.)
DELROY: You said the one in the kitchen only plays when it feels like it. I bought it three weeks ago. I wanted to give it to you after the party. (He sets it down.) I am going back; the driver is waiting.
MAVIS: (standing, folding the clothes mechanically) Delroy.
DELROY: (at the door) Yes, Mama.
MAVIS: (not looking at him) The door was never locked.
(He nods slowly. She folds the last shirt. He leaves. She sits down next to the radio and does not switch it on.)

Commentary: I ended with a stage direction rather than a line of dialogue because the original scene's power comes from what the characters cannot say. I gave Delroy an ordinary gift so that the argument about money is resolved by generosity instead of apology. I repeated the object of the parcel, and I placed the radio between them on the table as a physical symbol of the affection neither character states.
markScheme: Content and engagement (8 marks): a response that grows convincingly out of the original text and resolves its tension.
Craft and technique (8 marks): deliberate use of the conventions of drama or prose - dialogue, stage directions, sensory detail, point of view.
Language (5 marks): controlled vocabulary, sentences varied for effect, appropriate register.
Commentary (4 marks): three clear, accurate explanations of the writer's own choices.
examinerTips: In a creative response, technique is being marked, not just invention. Plan the ending first, use one object to carry the feeling, and leave something unsaid.
